deep.reconstruction:
Theorem (Lehrsatz): let a and b be coprime integers, and let x and y be arbitrary integers. Then the two numbers ax+by and ay−bx are either both divisible by N = a²+b², or neither is.

Proof as written.
(1) Gauss writes down two identities:
  (a−bi)(x+iy) = (ax+by) + (ay−bx)i
  (a+bi)(α−βi) = (aα+bβ) + (bα−aβ)i
(2) He multiplies them. The left side is (a−bi)(a+bi)(x+iy)(α−βi) = (a²+b²)[(αx+βy) + (αy−βx)i].
(3) For the right side, put A = ax+by, B = ay−bx, C = aα+bβ, D = bα−aβ. Expanding (A+Bi)(C+Di) gives:
  real part AC − BD = (aα+bβ)(ax+by) + (aβ−bα)(ay−bx)
  imaginary part AD + BC = (aα+bβ)(ay−bx) + (ax+by)(bα−aβ)
(4) Because gcd(a,b)=1, one can choose integers α, β with aα+bβ = 1 (Bézout). This is the only place the coprimality is used, and the step is left implicit. Comparing real and imaginary parts then gives:
  (I)  (a²+b²)(αx+βy) + (bα−aβ)(ay−bx) = ax+by
  (II) (a²+b²)(αy−βx) − (bα−aβ)(ax+by) = ay−bx
(5) Equation (I) shows that if N divides ay−bx, it divides ax+by. Equation (II) gives the converse.

What this serves (my interpretation): with N = a²+b², the identity is (a−bi)(x+iy) = A + Bi. The theorem says that N divides the real part of this product exactly when it divides the imaginary part, i.e. exactly when a+bi divides x+iy in Z[i]. Equivalently, for coprime a, b the ring Z[i]/(a+bi) behaves like Z/N, so a single rational congruence decides divisibility by the Gaussian integer a+bi.

This is a preparatory lemma for Gauss's theory of residues modulo a Gaussian integer a+bi. The neighbouring pages concern biquadratic reciprocity and complete residue systems mod a+ib. A shorter proof also exists (mine, not Gauss's): b(ax+by) + a(ay−bx) = Ny and a(ax+by) − b(ay−bx) = Nx. So if N divides one of the two numbers, N divides b times the other and a times the other, and gcd(a, b) = 1 lets you conclude via Bézout. Gauss's proof via Gaussian multiplication is, in effect, this argument.
errors: No mathematical errors. The real part on the right of the product identity is (aα+bβ)(ax+by) + (aβ−bα)(ay−bx), which is consistent with the final equation (I). In the manuscript this term is visibly overwritten or corrected, but the surviving reading (aβ−bα) is correct.
The use of gcd(a,b)=1, namely the existence of α, β with aα+bβ=1, is implicit. It is valid by Bézout.

results.what: For coprime a, b, a²+b² divides ax+by if and only if it divides ay−bx. Proved by multiplying (a−bi)(x+iy) by (a+bi)(α−βi) with aα+bβ=1.
results.modern_name: Elementary divisibility lemma in Z[i]: a Gaussian integer x+iy is divisible by a primitive a+bi iff N(a+bi) divides Re((a−bi)(x+iy)), equivalently Im. Related to Z[i]/(a+bi) ≅ Z/(a²+b²) for gcd(a,b)=1.
results.usually_credited_to: Folklore elementary number theory. It is implicit in Gauss's own Theoria residuorum biquadraticorum (1828/1832) and in later Gaussian-integer theory.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine elementary lemma with a short proof. It is part of the groundwork for Gauss's well-known work on Gaussian integers and biquadratic residues, which is firmly credited to him. The only interest is seeing the auxiliary lemma worked out explicitly with Bézout coefficients.

checkable.asserts: Product identity with correct real part (aβ−bα)(ay−bx)

transcription_corrections: The struck or garbled term '([-aβ-bα-])(ay-bx)' in the product identity should read '(aβ − bα)(ay − bx)'. The manuscript shows a correction over this term, and the corrected value is aβ−bα.
'identische Gleichungen' (Gauss's spelling 'identische Gleichungs/Gleichungen') and 'beweiset' are faithful to the manuscript. Otherwise the transcription agrees with the image.
